note: Matthew Stafford has had an up-and-down season as the QB18 in fantasy points per game. Among 29 qualifying passers, he is 13th in yards per attempt, 17th in passing success rate, 22nd in highly accurate throw rate, and 18th in hero throw rate. Stafford could easily have a bounceback game this week with strong QB1 production as he attempts to keep pace with Josh Allen. Buffalo has allowed the fifth-most passing yards, the 14th-highest yards per attempt, the seventh-highest passing success rate, and the sixth-most fantasy points per dropback.

Jacoby Brissett has been a low-aDOT point guard under center as the QB21 in fantasy points per game. He could flirt with QB1 production this week, though. That's how bad the Lions' pass defense has been. Among 29 qualifying quarterbacks, Brissett has the lowest yards per attempt, the sixth-lowest aDOT, the seventh-lowest deep ball rate, and the eighth-lowest hero throw rate while ranking 14th in passing success rate. He faces a Detroit pass defense that has given up the seventh-most yards per attempt, the third-highest passing success rate and CPOE, and the fifth-most fantasy points per dropback.

Drake Maye bounced back in a big way last week as the QB1 for the week. Josh McDaniels changed up the offense, and Maye responded in a big way. In Weeks 1-3, New England had the seventh-lowest motion rate and the fifth-lowest play-action rate. Well, last week, New England was fourth in motion rate (75.3%) and ninth in play-action rate (33.3%). Last week, Maye had the 12th-best passing success rate and 11th-best EPA per dropback when New England utilized motion. I expect the Pats to continue to utilize these playcalling cheat codes moving forward. Maye also ran seven times for 47 yards on the ground, which were the most rushing attempts and rushing yards for Maye since Week 1. Last week, among 32 qualifying quarterbacks, Maye was 17th in yards per attempt, 12th in passing success rate, and 20th in highly accurate throw rate. The Raiders have been a mixed bag as a pass defense, allowing the 13th-highest passing success rate, the fifth-lowest EPA per dropback, and ranking 16th in yards per attempt. The heavy inclusion of motion won't be as big of a cheat code for Maye and the Pats this week, though. The Raiders have allowed the fourth-fewest yards per attempt and the second-lowest EPA per dropback to motion. Maye could continue his bounce back this week, but it'll be a tougher climb up that hill this week.

Jayden Daniels practiced in full to open this week (elbow). I'm expecting him to be back this week. He'll be wearing a brace on his non-throwing arm. We'll see how this injury impacts his rushing, but I wouldn't be shocked to see him run less until this injury is further in the rearview mirror. In Week 1, Daniels was the QB13 in weekly scoring while rushing five times for 31 yards on the ground. Daniels has only 5.1 yards per attempt, a 66.7% catchable target rate, and a 56.9% highly accurate throw rate this season. None of those are good passing/accuracy metrics. Despite all of that, Daniels could dismantle the Giants' pass defense this week. New York has allowed the fifth-most passing touchdowns while ranking 16th in passing success rate and 18th in CPOE.

Jordan Love is the QB16 in fantasy points per game with two outings this season with at least 19 fantasy points. Love has been struggling all season as a passer behind a patchwork offensive line. Among 29 qualifying passers, Love has the 11th-fewest yards per attempt, the tenth-lowest passing success rate, the fourth-highest off-target rate, and the fifth-lowest catchable target rate. I don't see this as a bounceback opportunity for Love, as Chicago's pass defense has surprised so far this season, allowing the fifth-lowest passing success rate, the third-fewest passing touchdowns, and the third-lowest CPOE and EPA per dropback.

Bo Nix has played some bad football this season as the QB22 in fantasy points per game. He has one game this season with more than 16 fantasy points, and his passing accuracy metrics have been horrible. Among 29 qualifying passers, Nix has the third-fewest yards per attempt, the sixth-lowest passing success rate, the sixth-lowest highly accurate throw rate, and the sixth-highest turnover-worthy throw rate. Yep, there's nothing pretty there. I'd love to craft a positive Nix blurb here, but it's tough to believe in him at the moment. The matchup is quite nice this week, though, so we should expect at least decent QB2 value this week. The Bolts defense has mirrored their offense in dysfunction, giving up the eighth-most yards per attempt, the ninth-highest passing success rate, the eighth-highest CPOE, and the 14th-most fantasy points per dropback.

The Saints' only means of moving the ball these days is through the air and with the arm of Tyler Shough. Shough has directed a pass-happy Saints offense as the QB5 in fantasy points per game. Among 29 qualifying quarterbacks, he is 20th in yards per attempt, 13th in passing success rate, 18th in highly accurate throw rate, fifth in hero throw rate, and tenth in catchable target rate. He has played quite well, especially considering the circumstances around him. Shough will have a VERY tough week against a ferocious Minny defense. Minnesota has allowed the tenth-fewest yards per attempt, the lowest passing success rate, and the lowest EPA per dropback. They have the highest pressure rate while sporting the highest blitz rate (72.1%) in the NFL. Shough has navigated the blitz well this season, ranking 14th in yards per attempt and eighth in passing success rate, but this will be a tall order to overcome this week. Shough can still post good numbers for fantasy purposes this week merely because of the passing volume he'll see, but it won't be pretty at times.

After his QB5 finish last week in weekly scoring, C.J. Stroud is the QB15 in fantasy points per game. Stroud is quietly reminding people of the talent that he displayed during his rookie season. Among 29 qualifying passers, Stroud is ninth in yards per attempt, tenth in highly accurate throw rate, sixth in hero throw rate, and he has zero turnover-worthy throws. Stroud should cook again this week. The Titans' pass defense has been Swiss cheese this season. Tennessee is allowing the tenth-most yards per attempt, the 12th-highest passing success rate, and the fifth-most EPA per dropback. Tennessee will allow Stroud plenty of clean pockets this week, as they have the fifth-lowest pressure rate and the lowest quick pressure rate in the NFL.

Kyler Murray has been gawd awful over the last two weeks as the QB28 and QB27 in weekly scoring. He has averaged only four rushing attempts and 16.5 rushing yards per game in that span, so his legs haven't been utilized enough to make up for his putrid passing. Among 29 qualifying passers, Murray has the lowest passing success rate, the fifth-fewest yards per attempt, the seventh-lowest aDOT, and the tenth-lowest highly accurate throw rate and catchable target rate. Maybe the Saints are his "get right" elixir this week, but I have my doubts. New Orleans has allowed the sixth-highest passer rating, the fourth-highest passing success rate, the sixth-most EPA per dropback, and the tenth-most fantasy points per dropback.

Sam Darnold is the QB24 in fantasy points per game with one QB1 outing this season. Among 29 qualifying passers, Darnold ranks fourth in yards per attempt, 16th in passing success rate, 14th in highly accurate throw rate, and sixth in catchable target rate. He has not played poorly, but he has seen some dips in his per-dropback efficiency this season. This was to be expected with the change in offensive coordinator in the offseason, but he was also so ridiculously efficient last season that some regression was bound to take place in 2026. Sit Darnold this week. He isn't on the streaming radar against a pass defense that has allowed the third-fewest yards per attempt, the ninth-lowest passing success rate, and the second-fewest fantasy points per dropback.

Jalen Hurts is the QB12 in fantasy points per game, but he is one of the few healthy players left standing in the Eagles entering Week 5, and his rushing production has declined. Hurts has averaged only 5.3 rushing attempts and 26.3 rushing yards while not eclipsing 25 rushing yards in a game since Week 1. Among 29 qualifying passers, Hurts has struggled with the seventh-fewest yards per attempt, the fourth-lowest passing success rate, the sixth-highest off-target rate, and the third-lowest highly accurate throw rate. Hurts could have a bounce-back week against a secondary that has allowed the second-most yards per attempt and the tenth-highest passing success rate, but I'm a little hesitant to believe that, as the Jags have also limited passers to the fewest passing touchdowns (tied with Minnesota) and the fifth-fewest fantasy points per dropback.

Aaron Rodgers has flashed signs of fantasy life over the last two weeks with QB8 and QB3 performances in weekly scoring. Rodgers has been doing his best Jameis Winston impression since Week 3. Over the last two weeks, among 27 qualifying passers, Rodgers has been seventh in yards per attempt and has had the second-highest deep ball rate (third-highest aDOT), but he has also been 12th-worst in passing success rate, fifth-lowest in highly accurate throw rate, and the highest off-target rate. Essentially Rodgers has been saying every play, "well, ______ is down there somewhere...let it rip." We'll see how it works out for Jameis Rodgers this week, but the matchup is quite nice. Indy has allowed the fifth-most yards per attempt, the 11th-highest CPOE, and the ninth-most EPA per dropback.

Jalon Daniels was the QB21 last week on the strength of his eight carries for 55 yards. If he had scored a rushing touchdown, Daniels would have put up 19.4 fantasy points and finished as the QB11 for the week. The power of rushing production in fantasy can swing the day for quarterbacks even when their passing stats are mediocre. Daniels finished with only 148 passing yards, 4.9 yards per attempt, a 73.3% catchable target rate, and a 23.3% off-target rate (horrible). If Daniels can maintain this level of rushing production and marginally clean up the passing output, he could easily be a QB1 this week with a cakewalk matchup. Dallas has allowed the third-most yards per attempt, the highest passing success rate, and the fifth-highest CPOE.

Tyson Bagent didn't have a wondrous fantasy day in Week 4, but he was highly effective for the Bears. He passed for 268 yards with 7.9 yards per attempt and a 73.5% completion rate. He ran four times, but he only had one rushing yard. I'm not expecting him to add much with his legs this week. Last week, among 32 qualifying quarterbacks, Bagent was 11th in yards per attempt (sixth-lowest aDOT), fifth in passing success rate, sixth in catchable target rate, and 11th in EPA per dropback. Bagent could have another nice game this week, and if he gets the passing touchdowns along with it, he could flirt with QB1 fantasy production. Green Bay has allowed the 14th-highest passing success rate, the 12th-highest EPA per dropback, and has ranked 16th in CPOE.

Deshaun Watson is the QB13 in fantasy points per game with at least 19.7 fantasy points in two of his four starts. Watson has averaged 7.8 rushing attempts and 31.8 rushing yards to help pad his ceiling and floor weekly in fantasy. Watson continues to operate as a low-aDOT point guard. Among 29 qualifying passers, Watson has the 11th-most yards per attempt and the ninth-highest passing success rate, but he also has the lowest aDOT, the second-highest percentage of his passing yards arising from yards after the catch, and the tenth-highest turnover-worthy throw rate. Watson should have another serviceable QB2 outing this week against a pass defense that has given up the sixth-highest passing success rate, the 13th-most EPA per dropback, and has ranked 17th in CPOE.

Jameis Winston turned back the clock last week as the QB8 in fantasy. Last week, among 32 qualifying passers, Winston was fifth in yards per attempt, fourth in aDOT (11.3), 14th in passing yards (250), 21st in passing success rate, first in hero throw rate, and 25th in highly accurate throw rate. Yep, classic Jameis made a return. We'll see if we get this again this week, but the matchup with the Commanders sets up well for YOLO Winston to show his face again in Week 5. Washington has allowed the 13th-highest yards per attempt, the most passing touchdowns (tied), the 11th-highest EPA per dropback, and ranks 15th in passing success rate.

Kirk Cousins is the QB8 in fantasy points per game with at least 20 fantasy points in each of his last three starts. Cousins has rolled back the hands of time with his performance this season. Among 29 qualifying quarterbacks, he ranks 12th in passing success rate, 15th in yards per attempt and highly accurate throw rate, and 16th in catchable target rate. Cousins should still have a solid game this week, but it's a tough matchup, so I'd consider him a solid QB2, and anything more than that we get this week is icing on the cake. New England has allowed the eighth-fewest yards per attempt, the 13th-lowest passing success rate, the sixth-fewest EPA per dropback, and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per dropback.

Even though I had my offseason doubts about the Chargers offense, I don't even think in my wildest dreams I thought it would be this bad. Trevor Penning has a concussion. Joe Alt and Rashawn Slater are injured and unlikely to play this week. Justin Herbert is the QB30 in fantasy points per game and doesn't have a game this season with more than 14.3 fantasy points. I don't know if this is rock bottom for the Bolts, but it has to be close right? Among 29 qualifying passers, Herbert has the 12th-fewest yards per attempt, the fifth-lowest passing success rate, the third-highest turnover-worthy throw rate, and the fifth-fewest fantasy points per dropback. The Broncos will be without Patrick Surtain this week, which will help Herbert's cause, but I still don't have much faith in Herbert and this offense to get on track in Week 5. Denver has allowed the fifth-lowest passer rating, the sixth-lowest CPOE, and they have the tenth-best pressure rate. Good luck, Mr. Herbert.

Geno Smith is the QB23 in fantasy points per game. His only massively successful fantasy outing of the season was when he faced the Lions' woeful secondary. Last week, he had a horrible box score, but the Jets didn't have the ball. The Bears controlled the clock the entire game as the Jets only had the ball for 17:15. Smith finished with only 15 passing attempts. Smith has actually been playing quite well, and it hasn't been reflected in his box scores outside of destroying the Lions. Among 29 qualifying passers, Smith ranks eighth in yards per attempt, tenth in passing success rate, 12th in highly accurate throw rate, and first in catchable target rate. Smith is a middling QB2 this week. Cleveland's pass defense has played well, allowing the 13th-fewest EPA per dropback, the 14th-lowest passing success rate, and the ninth-lowest CPOE.

Michael Penix has only been asked to be a game manager during his first two starts of the season as Atlanta has been able to run the ball whenever they want and play with a lead. Penix has been the QB21 and QB24 in weekly fantasy scoring. Among 38 qualifying passers, Penix is first in yards per attempt, fourth in passing success rate, 15th in hero throw rate, and he has the 11th-lowest aDOT. He has only been pressured on 15.2% of his dropbacks, which is honestly insane. 62.6% of his passing yards have come from yards after the catch (fifth-highest rate). Penix is a run-of-the-mill QB2 again this week with a bad matchup. Baltimore has allowed the 12th-fewest yards per attempt, the 11th-lowest passing success rate, the seventh-fewest EPA per dropback, and the sixth-fewest fantasy points per dropback.

Daniel Jones continues to look like a statue in the pocket for the Colts as the QB36 in fantasy points per game. Jones hasn't been able to move in the pocket as he looks like 2025 Kirk Cousins. Among 29 qualifying passers, Jones has the second-fewest yards per attempt, the third-lowest aDOT, the lowest deep ball rate, and the ninth-highest turnover-worthy play rate. If Jones couldn't look competent against the Commanders last week, I don't know if he will during the 2026 season. After last week's face plant, I have zero faith that Jones can take advantage of a nice matchup this week. Pittsburgh has allowed the sixth-most yards per attempt, the fifth-highest passing success rate, and the 12th-highest CPOE. Jones is a low-end QB2 again this week.

Malik Willis has had a difficult beginning to the season. He has two games where his rushing production has been there with at least six rushing attempts and 39 rushing yards, while also having two games with only two rushing attempts and 12 or fewer rushing yards. This isn't going to get it done. If Willis is to have any fantasy value this season, Miami needs to dial up the rushing attempts for their quarterback. Willis is the QB34 in fantasy points per game. Among 29 qualifying passers, he has the 13th-lowest yards per attempt, the third-lowest passing success rate, the sixth-lowest catchable target rate, and the 11th-best hero throw rate. The arm talent is there, but the situation is gruesome, and he has faced the 12th-highest pressure rate. Willis has the potential for a solid game this week (if he can pile up some rushing production) against a Cincy pass defense that has allowed the 12th-most yards per attempt, the eighth-highest passing success rate, and the 14th-highest passer rating.

Last week, Tyler Huntley came in for Lamar Jackson and completed eight of nine passes with 7.0 yards per attempt. He ran the ball four times for 16 scoreless yards on the ground. Last year, in his two starts, Huntley averaged eight rushing attempts and 56.5 rushing yards, which isn't a surprise, as we know the rushing equity is there with Huntley. He was the QB16 and QB19 in weekly scoring in those starts with only two total passing touchdowns, zero rushing scores, and zero games with more than 200 passing yards. I wouldn't be shocked to see Huntley finish as a QB1 this week with his rushing upside, but he's best viewed as a high-floor QB2 with a tough matchup for Week 5. Atlanta's pass defense has been amazing, allowing the sixth-fewest yards per attempt, the fourth-lowest passing success rate, the tenth-fewest EPA per dropback, and the eighth-fewest fantasy points per dropback.

Cam Ward continues to work out his quarterbacking demons in real time this season as the QB27 in fantasy points per game. He has only one game with more than 17 fantasy points. Among 29 qualifying passers, Ward has the fourth-lowest yards per attempt, the eighth-lowest passing success rate, the fourth-lowest aDOT, and the lowest highly accurate throw rate. Houston's pass defense has been horrid to begin the season, but they are still pressuring the quarterback well, which could be Ward's undoing this week. Houston has allowed the seventh-most EPA per dropback, the tenth-most fantasy points per dropback, and the ninth-highest CPOE, but they also have the sixth-best pressure rate. Ward is a low-end QB2 again this week.

Jaylen Warren has been operating as Pittsburgh's bell cow in Rico Dowdle's absence. It sounds like Dowdle will be back this week. I have no clue how Pittsburgh will divvy up the workload between these two backs, but I lean toward Warren retaining the lead role at least for this week, with Dowdle likely being eased back in. Could it be a full-blown committee this week? It's possible, which is why I can't put Warren in the strong start category despite the fact that he's awesome and should retain the clear lead role, if not bell cow usage, even with Dowdle back. In Week 1, Warren had only a 36.5% snap share with 47.6% of the rushing attempts and a 31% route share (14.6% target share). Warren was the RB25 for the week with 15 touches and 73 total yards. Among 46 qualifying backs, Warren is 14th in explosive run rate, sixth in yards after contact per attempt, and fourth-best in missed tackle rate. Indy has allowed the 11th-highest rushing success rate, the seventh-most yards before contact per attempt, and the seventh-highest missed tackle rate. Warren could easily be anywhere from a solid flex to an RB1 this week. There's a wide range of outcomes here, as we have no clue about the division of labor for the backfield this week.

Aaron Jones has operated as Minnesota's bell cow since Week 2 as the RB16 in fantasy points per game. He hasn't played less than 73.1% of the snaps in any of those games, while averaging 23 touches and 108.4 total yards. Jones has volumed his way to productive fantasy days, but his efficiency remains horrible. Among 46 qualifying backs, Jones ranks 26th in explosive run rate, 34th in yards after contact per attempt, and 42nd in missed tackle rate. This week, that likely doesn't matter as he'll see another 20 touches and the matchup is amazing. The Saints have allowed the third-highest explosive run rate, the second-highest rushing success rate, and the sixth-highest missed tackle rate. I could list off probably 4-5 categories that the Saints suck in with defending the run, but what's the point? You get the gist here. They stink, and Jones should have plenty of room to scamper this week.

One week after operating as Arizona's bell cow, Jeremiyah Love was back into a frustrating committee in Week 4. Love talked about his body being tired post-game, which could be a reason for the backslide with the workload. He also picked up or exacerbated his ankle injury. He opened this week with a limited practice. Love played 46% of the snaps with a 53.8% rushing share and a 23.1% route share (2.9% target share). He finished with 15 touches and 55 total yards. Among 45 qualifying backs, Love ranks 16th in yards after contact per attempt and 30th in missed tackle rate. He faces a run defense that has allowed the highest explosive run rate, the 12th-highest rushing success rate, and the second-most yards before contact per attempt. Love's conditioning, health, and gamescript could be limiting factors for him this week.

I swear I'M NOT TILTING AT ALL! I'M NOT TILTING LAST WEEK! I promise. Ok, fine. I'll admit it. Watching Tuten get two touchdowns whipped off the board by holding calls and then watching Chris Rodriguez score last week made my face melt. Tuten finished with a disappointing 19 touches and 91 total yards when the fantasy box score should have been more grand. Tuten still finished with a season-high 59% snap share, 68% designed carry share, and 40.7% route share. Tuten has averaged 16.8 touches and 82.8 total yards as the RB17 in fantasy points per game. Tuten has another chance at a strong game this week. Philly ranks 17th in rushing success rate allowed while giving up the fifth-most yards after contact per attempt, and the second-highest missed tackle rate. This is a nice matchup for a back with Tuten's elusiveness.

I expect Braelon Allen to draw another start this week for the Jets with Breece Hall sidelined. Last week, Allen only finished as the RB33 in weekly scoring with 16 touches and 67 total yards, but he operated as the Jets' bell cow. Last week, Allen played 93.8% of the snaps with all of the rushing attempts and a 66.7% route share. Allen still hasn't been impressive on a per-touch basis with only a 3.1% explosive run rate, 1.88 yards after contact per attempt, and a 15% missed tackle rate. When he's seeing this type of volume and workload, it almost doesn't matter, though. The Browns' run defense will be more giving this week. Cleveland has allowed the second-highest explosive run rate, the sixth-most yards after contact per attempt, and the 12th-highest missed tackle rate. Allen should be a solid RB2 this week.

Cam Skattebo's Week 4 stat line looked much better in totality than it should have. Skattebo finished with 19 touches, 66 total yards, a 62.3% snap share, 64.3% of the rushing attempts, and a 45.5% route share (3.4%). This was thanks to a Najee Harris fumble in the fourth quarter of last week's game. In the first three quarters, Skattebo had a 55.6% snap share with 55.6% of the rushing attempts (Najee Harris: 38.9% of the rushing attempts). Harris had three red zone carries last week while Skattebo had only two. Harris is eating into Skattebo's workload somewhat. Skattebo's 2.16 yards after contact per attempt and 15% missed tackle rate are still passable but not amazing numbers. Skattebo remains a low-end RB2/flex this week, but he has a tough matchup, so he'll likely need a touchdown to pay off for fantasy. Washington has allowed the 12th-lowest explosive run rate, the 12th-fewest yards before contact per attempt, and the fifth-fewest yards after contact per attempt.

Quinshon Judkins is the RB21 in fantasy points per game now after seeing a bump in the passing game last week and getting into the end zone. Judkins has averaged 18.6 touches and 68 total yards. Judkins has a 36% route share this season with a 13.9% target share. Last week, his route share was still in line with this usage with a 36.1% mark, but he had a 21.9% target share. I don't expect that type of passing game usage to repeat, but I could easily be wrong. Judkins did see a 16.7% target share in Week 2, so maybe he does see somewhere in this area code of passing usage weekly moving forward. Judkins remains inefficient with his workload. Among 46 qualifying backs, he is 43rd in explosive run rate, 31st in yards after contact per attempt, and 21st in missed tackle rate. Much like with Braelon Allen, Judkins is seeing enough volume that it doesn't matter most weeks, especially when he gets in the end zone. Judkins should have another solid RB2 week. The Jets have allowed the seventh-highest rushing success rate, the sixth-most yards before contact per attempt, and the third-highest missed tackle rate.

Last week, Emanuel Wilson was the RB6 in fantasy as Seattle's lead back. I expect him to hold that role again this week. Last week, Wilson played 58.6% of the snaps with a 63.6% rushing share, a 34.6% route share, and an 18.2% target share. He finished with 24 touches and 120 total yards (two scores). Wilson has been fairly efficient with this workload. Among 46 qualifying rushers, he ranks 23rd in yards after contact per attempt and 18th in missed tackle rate. Wilson should have success again this week against a 49ers' run defense that has allowed the 13th-highest rushing success rate, the tenth-highest yards before contact per attempt, and the 11th-highest gap rushing success rate (Wilson: 41.5% gap).

Last week, Bucky Irving maintained his lead back role with a 55.7% snap rate, 38.9% route share, 16 touches, and 61 total yards. He didn't draw a target last week. The most worrisome part of his usage last week was that he split snaps with Kenneth Gainwell (25%) and Sean Tucker (37.5%) in the red zone. Irving had a 37.5% snap rate inside the 20-yard line last week while logging two red zone rushing attempts, with Tucker finishing with three. This is a horrible outcome for Irving's touchdown prospects weekly if it continues. Irving's per-touch metrics have started to dip from a strong start, which tells me he likely isn't 100% healthy. Among 45 qualifying backs, he is 29th in yards after contact per attempt and 28th in missed tackle rate. We'll see if Irving can bounce back this week. He has a nice matchup in front of him. Dallas has allowed the fourth-highest explosive run rate, the ninth-highest rushing success rate, and the 14th-most yards after contact per attempt.

It sounds like Rhamondre Stevenson is going to play in Week 5. He sustained a knee injury last week and has had limited practices all week. He has been listed as questionable. This season, Stevenson has had a 52.7% snap rate with a 29.2% rushing share and 47.2% route share (10% target share) in games with TreVeyon Henderson active. I'd expect similar usage or a full-on split between them, with a slight edge to Stevenson on passing downs. Among 46 qualifying rushers, Stevenson ranks 31st in explosive run rate, 22nd in yards after contact per attempt, and 38th in missed tackle rate. He hasn't been his usual efficient self through four weeks. With him being less than 100%, I'm not expecting that to change this week. He has split the red zone rushing work evenly with Henderson, with each back getting two carries inside the 20-yard line. Stevenson should see double-digit opportunities this week as a flex play in a good matchup. Las Vegas has allowed the ninth-highest explosive run rate, the second-most yards before contact per attempt, and the tenth-highest rushing success rate.

David Montgomery continues to split the backfield work with Woody Marks. Since Week 2, Montgomery has had a 57.8% snap rate, a 46.6% rushing share, a 43% route share, and a 3.5% target share. Over the last three weeks, he has averaged 10.3 touches and 38.3 total yards. Montgomery has only a 2.4% explosive run rate, 1.68 yards after contact per attempt, and a 15% missed tackle rate, but he has no running room. Montgomery has seen only 1.02 yards before contact per attempt and has been hit at or behind the line of scrimmage with 55.3% of his carries. I don't see Montgomery finding any more running room this week. Tennessee has allowed the eighth-lowest explosive run rate and yards per carry, the sixth-fewest yards before contact per attempt, and the 13th-lowest EPA per rush.

RJ Harvey has retained his passing-down role for Denver, with some early-down work sprinkled in. Harvey has a 43.3% snap rate with a 19.4% rushing share and a 42.9% route share (20.2% target share). He has averaged 10.3 touches and 60.3 total yards. Harvey hasn't been effective on early downs with zero explosive runs, 1.92 yards after contact per attempt, and only an 8% missed tackle rate. Among 29 qualifying backs, he has been awesome as a receiver, though, ranking first in target share, first in yards per route run, fifth in receiving yards, and seventh in first-read share. Harvey is flex-worthy again this week. The Bolts have allowed the 13th-most receiving fantasy points per game to running backs.

Last week, the Chargers backfield became a disgusting three-way committee. Hampton was third among the backs in snaps with 32.4%, second in rushing share (28.1%), and third in route share (24.4%). Hampton finished with 11 touches and 53 total yards. It was his lowest touch count of the season. Every week feels like a new frustrating low for Hampton as Mike McDaniel continues to do goofy stuff. The most frustrating part about all of it is that Hampton hasn't been bad when he has carried the rock. Among 46 qualifying rushers, he ranks 18th in explosive run rate and eighth in yards after contact per attempt. If they give Hampton more volume this week, behind a degraded offensive line, he could still have a nice day (possibly). Denver hasn't been able to stop anyone on the ground. The Broncos have allowed the fifth-highest explosive run rate, the second-most yards after contact per attempt, and the highest missed tackle rate.

With Tank Bigsby on the IR and Saquon Barkley injured, Will Shipley will take over as Philly's lead back until Barkley returns. Shipley hasn't been impressive when on the field during his NFL tenure. Since 2024, with his 59 NFL carries, Shipley has only a 1.8% explosive run rate, 1.63 yards after contact per attempt, and an 8% missed tackle rate. None of that is good or encouraging. Shipley should still see 12-15 touches for the Eagles, so there is some fantasy value here based on volume alone. Shipley is a volume-based flex play this week with a horrible matchup. The Jags have allowed the third-lowest explosive run rate, the ninth-lowest rushing success rate, the lowest missed tackle rate, and the fewest yards after contact per attempt.

Alvin Kamara reinjured his knee last week, but he was able to finish the game. Kamara popped up on the injury report with a back issue this week. He didn't practice on Wednesday, but he had limited sessions the rest of the week. He has been listed as questionable. Kamara clearly isn't 100%, but I still expect him to lead the backfield in touches this week. Kamara has only a 4.3% explosive run rate, 1.64 yards after contact per attempt, and an 8% missed tackle rate. There's nothing good to see here. Last week, he scored two touchdowns, which powered his RB9 finish for the week as he had only 12 touches for 58 total yards. Minnesota has allowed the third-lowest rushing success rate, the tenth-fewest rushing yards over expectation, and has the third-highest stuff rate. Kamara is a touchdown-dependent flex this week with a horrible matchup.

Last week, Ollie Gordon led the way for Miami's rushing attack with a 56.8% snap rate, a 50% rushing share, a 35% route share, and an 11.8% target share. Gordon finished with 11 touches and 100 total yards as the RB16 for the week. Gordon was running through some massive holes, as he had 4.78 yards before contact per attempt. I don't think that he sees anything close to that weekly, so take the massive game with a grain of salt. With the small sample of work this season, Gordon has 3.34 yards after contact per attempt, but his 14% missed tackle rate is more indicative of his elusiveness than the gaudy yards after contact per attempt number. With all of that said, Gordon could have another nice RB2 week against Cincy this week. Cincy has allowed the 11th-highest explosive run rate, the ninth-most yards after contact per attempt, and the fourth-highest missed tackle rate.

Jacory Croskey-Merritt is the RB36 in fantasy points per game, averaging 15.3 touches and 49.3 total yards. Bill has a 46.5% snap share with 47.5% of the rushing attempts and a 25% route share (5.1% target share). His rushing metrics have suffered behind Washington's horrible offensive line. Bill has only a 3.7% explosive run rate, 1.84 yards after contact per attempt, and a 5% missed tackle rate. He has another nice matchup this week, but I doubt his ability to find space again this week behind this offensive line. He has only 0.96 yards before contact per attempt. The line isn't even giving him a hard before contact while he also has a 53.6% rate of getting hit at or behind the line of scrimmage. New York has allowed the 12th-highest explosive run rate, the third-highest rushing success rate, and the fifth-most yards before contact per attempt. Bill should see enough volume to be at least flex-viable.

Since Week 2, Tony Pollard has been the RB24 in fantasy points per game, averaging 18 touches and 70.3 total yards. Over the last three weeks, Pollard has had a 54.2% snap rate, a 61.8% rushing share, and a 29.2% route share (9.2% target share). Among 45 qualifying backs, Pollard is 17th in explosive run rate and 14th in yards after contact per attempt. Pollard is only a volume-based flex this week that likely needs a touchdown to pay off for fantasy GMs. Houston has remained a top-tier run defense, allowing the seventh-lowest explosive run rate, the 13th-lowest rushing success rate, and the 11th-fewest yards after contact per attempt.

TreVeyon Henderson will split the workload with Rhamondre Stevenson again this week. In their three games together this season, Henderson has had a 43.5% snap rate, a 42.7% rushing share, and a 31.1% route share (2.2% target share). I'd expect Henderson to help out more on early downs this week, with Stevenson taking more of the passing downs. Henderson continues to be an underwhelming pro as a rusher. Among 46 qualifying backs, he ranks 28th in explosive run rate, 33rd in yards after contact per attempt, and 32nd in missed tackle rate. He'll likely flirt with double-digit touches this week as a passable flex option. Henderson has split the red zone work with Stevenson, with both backs seeing two red zone rushing attempts this season. Las Vegas has allowed the ninth-highest explosive run rate, the second-most yards before contact per attempt, and the tenth-highest rushing success rate.

Last week, J.K. Dobbins had his usual early down only role with a 31.3% snap share, 50% of the rushing attempts, and a 15.9% route share. Dobbins finished with 13 touches and 52 total yards, which is about the same workload that he has had in most weeks. The problem for Dobbins, outside of the Denver defense taking a huge step back this season, is that he doesn't resemble the same back that we have loved over the last few years. Dobbins has only a 4.9% explosive run rate and 11% missed tackle rate. Those are a shell of his former rushing metrics. Unfortunately for Dobbins, the Bolts have had a formidable run defense this year, and he's a sit this week. The Bolts have allowed the 11th-lowest explosive run rate, the fifth-lowest rushing success rate, and they have the sixth-best stuff rate.

Tyler Allgeier was back in the mix last week with a 54% snap rate, a 30.8% rushing share, a 33.3% route share, and a 5.7% target share. Allgeier finished with ten touches and 49 total yards (one score). I expect Allgeier to flirt with 10-12 touches again this week as a solid flex play. Among 45 qualifying rushers, Allgeier ranks tenth in yards after contact per attempt and 32nd in missed tackle rate. If he can get into the end zone again this week, he'll pay off for fantasy managers. He faces a run defense that has allowed the highest explosive run rate, the 12th-highest rushing success rate, and the second-most yards before contact per attempt.

Woody Marks continues to cut into David Montgomery's workload. Since Week 2, Marks has had a 42.2% snap rate, a 32.8% rushing share, a 35.2% route share, and a 7% target share. He has averaged 8.3 touches and 26 total yards. Marks has only 1.64 yards after contact per attempt, but he has logged a strong 25% missed tackle rate despite his offensive line only generating 1.46 yards before contact per attempt for him. Marks remains a touchdown-or-bust flex this week. Tennessee has allowed the eighth-lowest explosive run rate and yards per carry, the sixth-fewest yards before contact per attempt, and the 13th-lowest EPA per rush.

With Chris Brooks out this week, MarShawn Lloyd becomes an interesting desperation flex play. Last week, he led the backfield with a 54.5% snap share and 46.7% route share (16.7% target share). Yes, he was second among the group with a 28% rushing share, but that could change this week. Lloyd's 1.40 yards after contact per attempt isn't great, but he has only seen 1.30 yards before contact per attempt behind Green Bay's horrendous offensive line. Lloyd also has a solid 20% missed tackle rate, which is quite strong, and he posted 2.57 YPRR last week with that season-high 46.7% route share. Lloyd could surprise this week. The Bears' run defense has been awful, allowing the eighth-highest explosive run rate, the highest rushing success rate, and the third-most yards before contact per attempt.

Brian Robinson Jr. has essentially been Blake Corum of yesteryear over the last two weeks as the Falcons have leaned heavily on their ground game while playing with leads. Over the last two weeks, Robinson has finished as the RB19 and RB8 in weekly scoring while averaging 12.5 touches and 58.5 total yards with four touchdowns. Robinson has been quite good with the work he has received. Among 46 qualifying rushers, he is fifth in yards after contact per attempt and 16th in missed tackle rate. Robinson is a viable flex again this week, but he'll need another touchdown to pay off for fantasy purposes, with a tougher matchup likely. Baltimore has allowed the sixth-lowest rushing success rate, the seventh-fewest yards after contact per attempt, and the ninth-lowest missed tackle rate.

Blake Corum's role in the Rams' offense has evaporated. His snap share has dropped in each of the last three games, from 45.2% to 15.5% last week. Last week, he finished with only six touches and 21 total yards. Corum still doesn't have a red zone carry this season. He isn't on the flex radar until his role changes. Kyren Williams looks like a bell cow again.

Alvin Kamara is banged up. He reinjured his knee last week, but he was able to finish the game. He also popped up on the injury report with a new back issue this week. Kamara had a DNP to open the week. I'll update Kendre Miller's outlook on Friday. He could be the Saints' lead back this week.

Michael Wilson has emerged as Arizona's running mate with Trey McBride through the air as the WR20 in fantasy points per game. Wilson has a 27% target share, 1.69 YPRR, eight red zone targets (third among all wideouts), five deep targets, and a 35.7% first-read share. These are ELITE usage numbers, and his per-route efficiency is slowly ticking up too. Wilson should eat again this week. Detroit has allowed the sixth-most yards per target and the tenth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

In his two games played with Puka Nacua, Davante Adams has had a 19% target share with 0.81 YPRR (58 total receiving yards), two red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 23.2% first-read share. His other two games of the season have loudly displayed that Adams isn't near the end of the line, so this feels like small sample variance with his production dipping so much. His target share and first-read share were still strong in those games. I'm expecting a bounce-back performance for Adams in Week 5. Buffalo has the 11th-highest two-high rate (56.2%). This season against two-high, Adams has a 21% target-per-route run rate with 1.88 YPRR. His numbers are much better against single-high, but these aren't horrible metrics by any stretch of the imagination. Buffalo has allowed the eighth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Malik Nabers landed on the injury report this week (knee). He had soreness and didn't practice. His shoulder has been an issue, but we haven't seen his knee be a problem in the last few weeks, since he has been a full-time option. I'll update his outlook on Friday, but I wouldn't be surprised if Nabers misses Week 5.

Through four games, this has been a disappointing season for George Pickens as the WR39 in fantasy points per game. He has only one game with more than 15 PPR points. Last week, I thought we'd see the bounceback game for Pickens, but it didn't happen. What I didn't anticipate for Pickens was that Houston would absolutely abandon their single high ways for two-high (66% of their defensive snaps). We're going back to the single-high well with Pickens this week against a Bucs defense that has utilized single-high at the third-highest rate (66.2%). Overall, Pickens has an 18% target share, 1.65 YPRR, two red zone targets, five deep targets, and a 20.2% first-read share. Against single-high this season, Pickens has seen his target per route run rate climb from 14% to 35% and his YPRR increase from 1.41 to 2.30. If the Bucs continue their single high ways, Pickens should shred them. Tampa Bay has allowed the 11th-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 15th in yards per target against the position.

After last week's surprising dud, Parker Washington is the WR23 in fantasy points per game. Last week, Washington had only a 13% target share and a 14.3% first-read share as Trevor Lawrence was locked onto Brenton Strange. In the three previous weeks, Washington was the team's unquestioned alpha with a 27.2% target share, 3.25 YPRR, 0.132 FD/RR, and a 32.8% first-read share. This feels like an outlier instead of a signal to panic. Washington also faced DJ Turner with 63.6% of his routes last week. Turner held him to one target and zero receptions. Washington could bounce back this week. Philly ranks 17th in yards per target and 19th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to perimeter wide receivers, so this is more of a neutral matchup for Washington.

Matthew Golden continues with his sophomore breakout season as the WR16 in fantasy points per game. Among 77 qualifying receivers, Golden is 19th in separation and 30th in route win rate. Golden leads the team with a 22.7% target share and 27% first-read share with 2.03 YPRR, five red zone targets, and seven deep targets. This week, Golden faces a Chicago pass defense that has the fifth-highest single high rate (62.9%). Against single high, Golden has seen a strong 25% target per route run rate but his YPRR has slipped to 1.27. That's not great at all, but he should still see the volume this week with that strong target per route run rate. Golden and Christian are the team's top targets against single high. Golden should have a strong week against a secondary that has allowed the second-most yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Bo Nix and suspect play-calling have capsized this offense in most weeks so far. Jaylen Waddle is the WR34 in fantasy points per game. Waddle has a 19.3% target share, 1.70 YPRR, two red zone targets, four deep targets, and a 28.2% first-read share. It has been tough when you can see Waddle getting open on film, but he can't toss the ball to himself. If Bo Nix can get himself together this week, Waddle could have a nice game, but that's a huge question mark. The Chargers have allowed the seventh-most yards per target and the fifth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

DK Metcalf has had a predictably rough start to the season as the WR35 in fantasy points per game. He has rebounded somewhat over the last two games with at least 12.1 PPR points in each week. Metcalf has a 21.3% target share with 1.33 YPRR, one red zone target, ten deep targets, and a 29.6% first-read share. Metcalf has had some tough corner assignments to begin the season, but he has been woefully inefficient with his targets. We'll see if that changes this week against an Indy pass defense that has held perimeter wide receivers to the ninth-fewest yards per target and the fourth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity. I'm not hopeful for Metcalf this week.

Last week, with Tyson Bagent under center, Luther Burden was third on the team in target share (17.6%) and first-read share (17.4%). Burden finished with 63 receiving yards (2.63 YPRR) and one deep target (zero red zone targets). Overall, Burden leads the team with a 22% target share and 28.6% first-read share while logging 2.11 YPRR, six red zone targets, and a deep target. This week, Burden faces a Green Bay secondary that has the sixth-highest two-high rate in the NFL (62.1%). Over the last two weeks, against two high, Burden ranks third on the team with a 27% target-per-route run rate with 1.73 YPRR. Burden should have a solid week against a secondary that is 17th in fantasy points per opportunity against wide receivers.

Josh Downs had a quiet week last week with a good matchup, but I think the blame should be laid at the Achilles of Daniel Jones and not placed upon Downs. Jones has been quite limited as a passer so far this season. Downs is the WR48 in fantasy points per game with two games with at least 12.7 PRR points this season. Downs has a 20.5% target share, 1.67 YPRR, four red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 26.8% first-read share (leads the team). Among 45 qualifying receivers, Downs leads all of them in separation and ranks sixth in route win rate. We'll see if he can bounce back this week, but the matchup isn't great. Pittsburgh has allowed the 14th-fewest yards per target and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers.

After a massive Week 4 performance, Carnell Tate is the WR27 in fantasy points per game. Carnell Tate has been commanding alpha-level volume, and now we're starting to see it pay off. Among 79 qualifying receivers, Tate is seventh in target share (26.9%), 17th in YPRR (2.39), third in air-yard share (50.1%), 20th in FD/RR (0.098), and sixth in first-read share (36%). Tate has only one red zone target and three deep targets this season. Tate could be a strong WR3/flex again this week if Cam Ward can provide him catchable targets. Houston has allowed the third-most yards per target and the fourth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Jameson Williams had a boom game last week as the WR17 for the week. This week could be more of the same for the volatile big-play machine. Williams has a 14.9% target share, 1.45 YPRR, two red zone targets, six deep targets, and a 23.7% first-read share. Arizona has been bleeding out production to perimeter wide receivers, and Williams' splits this season are in favor of the heavy two-high coverage he'll see this week. Arizona has utilized two high at the second-highest rate in the NFL (73.2%). Against two-high, Williams has seen his target-per-route run rate climb from 14% to 16% and his YPRR increase from 1.32 to 1.57. Arizona has allowed the most yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Mike Evans is an absolute DAWG! Evans gutted it out last week with a myriad of injuries, including broken ribs. Evans grimaced and was slow to get up after every catch, but that didn't stop him. Evans is the WR24 in fantasy points per game, and he's been awesome when on the field for the 49ers. Last week, Evans had a 67.6% route share, a 26.7% target share, 3.30 YPRR, and a 31.3% first-read share. Overall, this season Evans has a 60.8% route share, a 21.2% target share (32% TPRR), 2.80 YPRR, four red zone targets, four deep targets, and a 24.7% first-read share. This week, he'll face a Seattle secondary that has utilized two high at the ninth-highest rate in the NFL (59.1%). Against two high, Evans has a 33% target-per-route run rate and 3.10 YPRR, which are absolutely elite numbers. Seattle has allowed the sixth-fewest yards per target and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers. Evans has the talent to overcome a bad matchup, though. In most leagues, I'm still starting him.

Malik Washington is the WR45, but over the last two games he has been the WR39 and WR35 in weekly scoring with volume alone. If you toss a touchdown on top of either of those stat lines, Washington would have been a WR2 in weekly fantasy scoring. Washington has a 27.2% target share, 1.99 YPRR, one red zone target, six deep targets, and a 28.3% first-read share. Washington is a volume-fueled flex again this week. The matchup isn't great, but I expect him to see a heavy target load, and if he finally gets in the endzone, he'll pay off for fantasy this week. Cincy has allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target and the ninth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to receivers.

Romeo Doubs fulfilled all of the offseason hope and promise last week as the WR8 for the week. Last week, Doubs had a 21.6% target share, 58 receiving yards (2.07 YPRR), three red zone targets (two scores), one deep target, and a 26.3% first-read share. Since Week 2, Doubs has had a 17.8% target share with 2.78 YPRR, four red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 19.2% first-read share. We'll see if Doubs can continue the production this week, but the coverage structure works in his favor. The Raiders have the tenth-highest rate of two-high (56.2%). Since Week 2, against two-high, Doubs has a 19% target-per-route run rate (leads the team) with 4.54 YPRR (WOW!). The Raiders are a middle-of-the-road matchup for Doubs, ranking 17th in yards per target allowed to perimeter wide receivers. Doubs could have another strong week against Vegas as Drake Maye's main weapon against two-high coverage.

Denzel Boston is the WR20 in fantasy points per game, while commanding an 18.3% target share with 2.39 YPRR, three red zone targets, seven deep targets, and a 22.5% first-read share (second on the team). Boston has excelled so far this season, ranking 17th in separation and YPRR while sitting at seventh in route win rate among 77 qualifying receivers. This week, he'll tangle with a Jets' secondary that has the fifth-highest two-high rate (62.2%). Against two-high, Boston leads the team with a 21% target-per-route run rate against two-high while logging 4.47 YPRR. This is a tougher matchup for Boston, but I think he can overcome it. The Jets have allowed the tenth-fewest yards per target to perimeter wide receivers while ranking 15th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to the position.

Deebo Samuel has been balling this season as the WR16 in fantasy points per game. Samuel has had some rushing production, padding his fantasy stats with seven carries and 74 yards on the ground. He has touchdowns in three of the 49ers' four games this season. Samuel has a 14.2% target share with 2.31 YPRR, five red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 15.1% first-read share. This week, he'll face a Seattle secondary that has utilized two high at the ninth-highest rate in the NFL (59.1%). Against two high, he has seen his numbers suffer this season, with Mike Evans and George Kittle leading the way against this coverage. Samuel has only a 15% TPRR and 1.11 YPRR against two high this season. With a tough matchup incoming this week, temper your expectations. Seattle has allowed the sixth-fewest yards per target and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

KC Concepcion leads the team with a 22.6% target share and 30% first-read share despite being the WR65 in fantasy points per game. Concepcion has been the higher-volume, low aDOT (4.96) receiver for Todd Monken's offense. He has 1.24 YPRR, three red zone targets (tied for the team lead), and two deep targets. The Jets have the fifth-highest two-high rate (62.2%). Against two-high, Concepcion is fourth on the team in target per route run rate (17%) and has only 0.67 YPRR. This isn't a great matchup for Concepcion, as the Jets have limited slot receivers to the tenth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity while ranking 15th in yards per target allowed to the position.

Khalil Shakir is the WR64 in fantasy points per game. His best performance of the season came last week as the WR24 in weekly scoring. Overall, Shakir has a 19.3% target share with 1.98 YPRR (65.4% route share), five red zone targets (zero scores), two deep targets, and a 23.4% first-read share. Shakir is flex-worthy again this week. The Rams are tied for the most receiving touchdowns allowed to slot receivers while also surrendering the seventh-most fantasy points per opportunity to the position.

Devaughn Vele has been a beneficiary of the Saints' pass-happy offense as the WR20 in fantasy points per game. Vele's per-route numbers are nothing impressive. He has a 17.2% target share, 1.30 YPRR, and a 22% first-read share, but the passing volume has helped him have some big box scores along with his six red zone targets and six deep targets. The high cholesterol usage has been wonderful, as he has two scores this season. This week, he faces a Minny defense that has utilized two high with 65.6% of their defensive snaps (fourth-highest rate). Against two-high, Vele has seen his target-per-route run rate drop to 16% with a dip to 1.03 YPRR. These numbers aren't great, and the matchup is tougher, but he could still see enough volume to have a nice flex day. Minnesota has allowed the eighth-fewest yards per target and the sixth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers.
Justin Jefferson is still recovering from an ankle injury. He opened this week with a limited practice. I'll update his outlook on Friday.

Jordan Addison was a surprise addition to the injury report with a hamstring injury. He opened the week with a DNP, but he had limited practices the rest of the week. He has been listed as questionable. In Weeks 1-2 with Justin Jefferson playing a full-time role, Addison had a 15.9% target share with 0.47 YPRR, one red zone target, and a 16.7% first-read share. He was the WR108 and WR78 in weekly scoring. The Saints are 16th in yards per target allowed to perimeter wide receivers while also giving up the sixth-most fantasy points per opportunity. Addison could be the third option in a wobbly passing attack led by Kyler Murray. He's a middling flex.

Last week, with Tyson Bagent chucking the rock, Rome Odunze was second on the team in target share (20.6%) and first-read share (21.7%). He finished with zero red zone targets and one deep target. Odunze led the team with 94 receiving yards (3.36 YPRR). Overall, Odunze has a 15.2% target share with 2.12 YPRR, two red zone targets, six deep targets (leads the team), and a 15.5% first-read share. This week, Odunze faces a Green Bay secondary that has the sixth-highest two-high rate in the NFL (62.1%). Over the last two weeks, against two high, Odunze has ranked second on the team with a wonderful 29% target-per-route run rate while posting 4.83 YPRR (OH BABY!). I wouldn't be surprised to see Odunze leading the way in the receiving department this week again. Green Bay is 17th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to perimeter wide receivers.

Last week, with DeVonta Smith sidelined, Dontayvion Wicks was third among Philly's starting wide receivers in target share with 14.8%, as he also tied for second among the group with a 22.2% first-read share. Wicks finished with 18 receiving yards (0.58 YPRR), zero red zone targets, and one deep target. He did have to deal with Trent McDuffie last week, with 51.6% of his routes. Against McDuffie, he had only one target, which he secured for seven receiving yards. In the previous three games, Wicks was involved with a 17% target share, 2.29 YPRR, and a 23.2% first-read share. This could be a nice bounceback spot for Wicks. In three of the Jags' four games, they have utilized two high with 56.7-56.9% of their defensive snaps. Against two-high, Wicks has an 18% target-per-route run rate and 2.31 YPRR. The Jags have only given up one receiving touchdown to perimeter wide receivers while surrendering the tenth-most yards per target to the position.

Jakobi Meyers is the WR37 in fantasy points per game with two outings with 12 or more PPR points. Meyers has a 14.4% target share, 1.85 YPRR, three red zone targets, one deep target, and a 17.7% first-read share. Trevor Lawrence has leaned on Meyers more over the last two games, as he has had a 23.1% target share, 2.16 YPRR, and a 29.3% first-read share during that span. Meyers is a viable flex this week with the increased usage. Philly ranks 17th in yards per target and 19th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to perimeter wide receivers.

In Jalon Daniels' first start, Emeka Egbuka found himself as the third option in the passing attack, finishing third on the team with a 14.8% target share and 19% first-read share behind Cade Otton and Chris Godwin. Egbuka finished with only 13 receiving yards and one red zone target. It was a disappointing showing for Egbuka. With Daniels still finding his footing, I'd love to craft a narrative that Egbuka immediately bounces back; I don't know if that happens, but it's possible. Dallas has been tougher against perimeter wide receivers, though, allowing the eighth-fewest yards per target and the 11th-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to the position. Egbuka is just a risky flex with upside this week.

Wan'Dale Robinson is the WR39 in fantasy points per game. He has commanded a 19.3% target share with 1.21 YPRR, a 24% first-read share, four red zone targets, and two deep targets. Robinson has at least 11 PPR points in each of his last two games. He's a viable PPR flex again this week. Houston has allowed the 13th-fewest yards per target to slot receivers while ranking 16th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to the position.

Outside of his outlier performance in Week 2, Tre Tucker hasn't surpassed 44 receiving yards in any game this season. Taking Week 2 out of the sample, Tucker has a 13.9% target share with 1.25 YPRR, one red zone target, four deep targets, and a 19.4% first-read share. Tucker is a deep league flex only against a secondary that has held perimeter wide receivers to the 13th-fewest yards per target, but also allowed the 12th-most fantasy points per opportunity to the position.
Keon Coleman has functioned as Buffalo's Rashod Bateman. He is essentially DJ Moore's handcuff. If Moore misses this week, Coleman could see a ton of work. I'll update his outlook on Saturday.

Tre Harris could be the only healthy receiver left standing this week among the Chargers' usual starting trio. Harris disappeared into the ether in Week 2 with what looks like an outlier quiet week in this passing attack. If we look at his three other games this season, he has been highly targeted in this broken passing attack. In those three other games, Harris has had a 19.4% target share with 1.93 YPRR, three red zone targets, two deep targets, and a 23.1% first-read share. This is a tough matchup for Harris, but Denver's coverage structure is in his favor. In three of Denver's four games, they have utilized single high with 51.7-55.9% of their defensive snaps. Against single high, Harris has a STRONG 24% target per route run rate and 2.88 YPRR this season. Harris could see enough volume this week to be flex-viable, and he has the talent to possibly overcome a rough matchup, but with how bad the Bolts offense has been, he's a risky option. There's no denying that. Denver has allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target and the sixth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers. The silver lining for Harris is that Patrick Surtain and Riley Moss (Denver's two starting outside corners) are out this week.

With the status of Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins up in the air for Week 5 and the fact that Colbie Young missed last week's game (knee), I'll update the outlook for this receiving depth chart on Saturday after we have more info.

As bad as things have been for Jaylen Waddle, they have been even worse for Courtland Sutton as the WR89 in fantasy points per game. Sutton has only a 14.8% target share, 0.77 YPRR, five red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 23.9% first-read share. Only 55% of his targets have been catchable. Despite a wonderful matchup this week, Sutton is a desperation flex only. The Chargers have allowed the seventh-most yards per target and the fifth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Roman Wilson has popped up out of nowhere to finish as the WR24 and WR18 in weekly scoring over the last two weeks. Since Week 3, Wilson has had a 17.6% target share, 3.83 YPRR, two red zone targets, five deep targets, and a 20.8% first-read share. This week, he could keep the hot streak rolling with a matchup against Indy's secondary that has allowed the second-most yards per target and the eighth-most fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers.

Last week, Kalif Raymond's role shrank as his route share dipped to 44.4% and his snap share fell to 47.2%. The offense looked like what we thought we were getting in the summer with Colston Loveland, Luther Burden, and Rome Odunze leading the way. With Tyson Bagent under center again this week, I can't confidently say that Raymond's role will bounce back, so I have to declare him a sit this week. If he bounces back and is an integral part of the passing attack this week, I won't be surprised, but a sub-50 % snap share last week with a 5.9% target share has me spooked that he also could easily give you a zero in your fantasy lineup in Week 5.

Last week, without DeVonta Smith, Makai Lemon had an 18.5% target share with 27 receiving yards (1.04 YPRR) and a 22.2% first-read share. Lemon is the WR94 in fantasy points per game without more than six PPR points in any game this season. Overall, Lemon has a 12.2% target share with 0.59 YPRR, zero red zone targets, one deep target, and a 14.9% first-read share. This could be a game where he offers flex value, but in most leagues I'm sitting him. In three of the Jags' four games, they have utilized two high with 56.7-56.9% of their defensive snaps. Against two-high, Lemon has had only a 12% target-per-route run rate and 0.25 YPRR. The Jags have allowed the tenth-most yards per target to slot receivers, but they haven't yielded a receiving touchdown to the position yet.

Last week, in Jalon Daniels first start, Chris Godwin had a team-leading 25.9% target share with a 23.8% first-read share (second on the team). Now, Godwin did nothing with the volume, with only 31 receiving yards and 1.03 YPRR, but it's notable that he was the team leader in target share. Last week, Godwin didn't see a red zone or deep target. Godwin could see his best game of the season against Dallas, though, if this usage holds for Week 5. Dallas has been ripped to shreds by slot receivers, giving up the highest yards per target and the fourth-most fantasy points per opportunity.

I don't care that Brian Thomas Jr. caught a touchdown in Week 4. He has been phased out of the offense with a 43.8% and 63% route share over the last two games. In those games, Thomas Jr. had target shares of 3.4% and 8.7% with first-read shares of 5% and 9.5%. Sit Thomas Jr. until his usage improves.

Last week, Chris Bell was so close to a big game, but he stepped out of bounds, and a massive play was called back. Don't let his quiet box score overshadow the fact that his route share was up to 80% last week. Bell also had a 17.6% target share and 16.7% first-read share. With his 93.8% snap rate on the perimeter last week, though I'm worried he sees a ton of DJ Turner this week, so I'm sitting him. Turner has followed DK Metcalf, Xavier Hutchinson, Emeka Egbuka, and Parker Washington on 52.9-77.1% of their routes this season. Only one of those receivers surpassed 31 receiving yards in Turner's coverage. Only Metcalf scored a touchdown because another Bengal ran into Turner. Sit Bell this week, but hopefully brighter days are ahead.

Isaac TeSlaa is a solid deep league flex this week. Last week, he finished with a season-high 95 receiving yards while seeing an 11.5% target share with one red zone target, two deep targets, and a 10.3% first-read share. The market share marks aren't amazing, but the matchup is wonderful, and the coverage structure is in his favor. Arizona has utilized two-high at the second-highest rate in the NFL (73.2%). Against two-high, TeSlaa has seen his target-per-route run rate increase from 8% to 15% and his YPRR jump from 0.48 to 2.52. Arizona has allowed the most yards per target and fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Last week, Darius Cooper finished as the WR13 for the week as he secured two touchdowns. Cooper had a 25.9% target share with 33 receiving yards (1.18 YPRR) and a 27.8% first-read share. Cooper had three red zone targets and two deep targets. Some of Cooper's high-volume usage could be related to the fact that Dontayvion Wicks was dealing with Trent McDuffie for more than half of the game. Cooper only had to deal with McDuffie for 25% of his routes. Cooper is an interesting deeper league flex this week. In three of the Jags' four games, they have utilized two-high with 56.7-56.9% of their defensive snaps. Against two-high, Cooper has had a massive 28% target-per-route run rate in his limited playing time with 1.44 YPRR. The Jags have only given up one receiving touchdown to perimeter wide receivers while surrendering the tenth-most yards per target to the position. Cooper is a desperation flex that could pay off this week.
Quentin Johnson opened this week with a limited practice (chest). He could be the Bolts' leading receiver this week or he could miss the game. I'll update his outlook on Friday.

Last week was the second time that Jaylin Noel has had above a 55% snap share and route share (60.3%, 60%). Noel saw a season-high 9.7% target share and 13.6% first-read share. When he has been on the field, Noel has been productive with 2.21 YPRR and 0.083 FD/RR, but Houston refuses to utilize him in a full-time role consistently. It's infuriating for a team that has obvious needs at pass catcher outside of Nico Collins. I don't know if Houston will continue to feature him more or if he'll get shoved back into an idiotic part-time role, but if he sees targets this week, he'll produce. Tennessee has allowed the third-most yards per target and the most fantasy points per opportunity to slot receivers (Noel: 73.8% slot).
Terry McLaurin missed last week's game with a late-week hamstring injury. He opened this week with a DNP (hamstring). I'll update his outlook on Friday, but I'm expecting him to miss Week 5.

Tee Higgins sustained groin and neck injuries last week. I fully expected Higgins to miss this week, but he had a full practice on Friday after missing practice the rest of the week. He has been listed as questionable. I'll update his outlook on Saturday. I'm hoping that we get more news on Higgins and Ja'Marr Chase on Saturday.

Keenan Allen missed last week's game with a groin injury. This week, he had limited practices on Wednesday and Thursday before upgrading to a full practice on Friday. He has been listed as questionable. Allen is the WR44 in fantasy points per game with one top-24 weekly finish this season (WR20). Allen has a 20.4% target share with 1.33 YPRR, three red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 26% first-read share. Daniel Jones' level of play is a big limiting factor for the Indy passing attack, and I don't see that changing this week. Despite that, Allen is a viable flex play this week as Pittsburgh has allowed the fourth-most yards per target and the sixth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.
DJ Moore reinjured or exacerbated his shoulder injury last week. I'll update his outlook on Saturday once we have practice reports to chew on.

Ladd McConkey hasn't practiced all week as he's dealing with a foot injury. He has been listed as questionable. I think he's closer to doubtful. I don't trust the Chargers injury reports at all, as we've seen too much goofy from them over the last two seasons. Even if McConkey is active (I doubt it), I'd expect him to be a limited-snap player with a bad matchup. Even without Patrick Surtain and Riley Moss, the Denver secondary is talented, and the Chargers don't have a healthy offensive line to hold their pass rush back from Justin Herbert. Sit McConkey. Denver has allowed the seventh-fewest yards per target and the sixth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter wide receivers.

Michael Pittman was seen using a scooter to move around the locker room on Wednesday. His foot was elevated. He was listed as a limited participant in practice on Wednesday, but I'm calling bs. Pittman is so limited with his foot that he needs the use of a scooter, but he suited up for practice? C'mon man. I'll update his outlook on Friday, but it's not looking good for him to play in Week 5.
Caleb Douglas looks like he'll be sidelined for another week (ankle). He opened this week with another DNP.

With the status of Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins up in the air for Week 5 and the fact that Colbie Young missed last week's game (knee), I'll update the outlook for this receiving depth chart on Saturday after we have more info. Young managed limited practices on Wednesday and Friday while logging a full session on Thursday.

Isaiah Likely has been crushing it as the TE6 in fantasy points per game. Likely has an 81.1% route share, a 30.4% target share, 1.84 YPRR, six red zone targets, two deep targets, and a 34.1% first-read share. He has been amazing. He should have another outstanding week against a defense that has allowed the third-most yards per target and the most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Harold Fannin is the TE8 in fantasy points per game with at least 10.4 PPR points in each of his last three games. Fannin has a 78.4% route share with a 20% target share, 1.40 YPRR, three red zone targets, one deep target, and a 16.3% first-read share. Temper your expectations for Fannin this week. The Jets have limited tight ends to the 11th-fewest yards per target and the seventh-fewest fantasy points per opportunity.

Juwan Johnson has been a steady fantasy producer with at least 10.8 PPR points in each game as the TE4 in fantasy points per game. Johnson has a 14.4% target share with 1.69 YPRR, seven red zone targets (WOW!), one deep target, and an 18.7% first-read share. The Vikings have faced the eighth-fewest tight end targets this season, but they have surrendered the tenth-highest yards per target to the position. Johnson should flirt with strong TE1 production again this week.

Well, this looked like what we thought we were getting in 2026 with Colston Loveland last week. While he didn't post a massive stat line, Loveland had a 66.7% route share and 91% snap share as he led the team with a 26.5% target share and 34.8% first-read share. Loveland had three red zone targets, 57 receiving yards, and 2.38 YPRR. This week, Loveland faces a Green Bay secondary that has the sixth-highest two-high rate in the NFL (62.1%). Over the last two weeks, against two high, Loveland has had an elite 35% target-per-route run rate and a strong 1.88 YPRR. Green Bay is 16th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to tight ends. The last time Loveland faced the Packers, he secured eight of his 15 targets with 137 receiving yards. I'm not saying that he'll post that type of stat line, but he could easily lead the team in targets again this week with Bagent slinging it around the yard.

Mike Gesicki is the TE13 in fantasy points per game with at least 12.7 PPR points in three of four games. He could see an elevated role this week with the state of the Cincy depth chart and injuries. If we take out his dude in Week 2, Gesicki has scored a touchdown in every other game. Excluding the stinker in Week 2, Gesicki has had a 54.8% route share, an 11.9% target share, a 20% target-per-route run rate, 2.09 YPRR, and a 12.6% first-read share. He has three red zone targets and two deep targets. Gesicki should shred the Miami secondary this week. The Dolphins have allowed the most yards per target and the fifth-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

TJ Hockenson is the TE11 in fantasy points per game. Hockenson has a 22.7% target share with 2.14 YPRR, four red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 23.5% first-read share. All of his per-route numbers and fantasy production are being inflated by his massive outing in Week 4, but he was also the TE9 in weekly scoring in Week 1 with Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison active. Hockenson could easily be the number two target in the Minny passing attack this week with a wonderful matchup and return TE1 production. New Orleans has allowed the fifth-most yards per target and the 12th-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Mark Andrews is the TE18 in fantasy points per game, but he finally finished as a TE1 last week (TE8). His per-route data has been awesome, though. Yes, among 46 qualifying tight ends, he ranks 16th in route share (67.5%), but also in that same sample he is fourth in target share (22.9%), 12th in YPRR (1.80), and fifth in first-read share (26%). Andrews has three red zone targets and one deep target. Andrews could easily be a TE1 again this week. Atlanta is 14th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to tight ends, while surrendering 15.6 PPR points to Pat Freiermuth, 18.3 PPR points to Darren Waller, and 11.9 PPR points to Juwan Johnson this season. Those three tight ends combined for three scores, and Johnson could have easily had a score at the end of the game last week, but the target went to Devaughn Vele.

With Mason Taylor back this week, Kenyon Sadiq is likely tossed right back into a frustrating tight end committee situation. In Weeks 1-2, with Taylor active, Sadiq had only a 39.3% snap share, 41.3% route share, and 7.7% target share. Maybe he sees more work this week than that with Adonai Mitchell still sidelined, but it's not a certainty. The Browns are 15th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to tight ends while also giving up the 13th-fewest yards per target to the position. Sadiq is a must-sit this week with a middle-of-the-road matchup and questionable usage for Week 5.

Hunter Henry is the TE29 in fantasy points per game. His best finish in weekly scoring was last week as the TE16 in fantasy. Since Week 2, Henry has had a 12.2% target share with 1.47 YPRR, one red zone target, one deep target, and a 17.3% first-read share. Henry is a viable streaming option this week. Vegas has been allowing a ton of production to tight ends, giving up the fifth-most receiving fantasy points per game and the second-most receiving touchdowns (tied) to the position.

Jake Ferguson is the TE22 in fantasy points per game with only one huge game this season. Ferguson has only one outing with more than ten PPR points this season. Ferguson has only a 10% target share with 0.76 YPRR, four red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 9.6% first-read share. Outside of his touchdown equity in this Dallas passing attack, he has been a forgotten player. Maybe that changes this week, but I'm not holding my breath. The matchup is nice for Ferguson, so he's on the streaming radar. He's a touchdown-or-bust option, though. Tampa Bay has allowed the ninth-most yards per target and the tenth-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Dalton Schultz has seen his route share decline weekly. In Week 1, he was rocking a 73.8% route share, but last week he was down to 60%. Does it make any sense? Nope, but hey, it's the Texans, and none of their player usage makes any sense. Schultz has an 18.4% target share with 1.83 YPRR, two red zone targets, three deep targets, and a 19.4% first-read share. He has been the consistent WR2 for the offense despite his declining playing time. Schultz is a viable streaming tight end option. Tennessee's season-long stats are good against tight ends, but they haven't really been tested with injuries and bad quarterback play until last week. Mark Andrews and Matthew Hibner secured seven of their eight targets last week with 61 receiving yards and a score. Schultz could produce low-end TE1 numbers in Week 5.

Brenton Strange is the TE21 in fantasy points per game after finishing as the TE5 in weekly scoring last week. Strange has a 17.3% target share with 2.04 YPRR, two red zone targets, zero deep targets, and a 19% first-read share. I expect this to be a quieter week for Strange against a defense that has allowed the 12th-fewest yards per target and the sixth-fewest fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends.

Pat Freiermuth is the TE18 in fantasy points per game with two outings this season with 10.7 PPR points or more. Freiermuth has a 63.2% route share, which has dipped below 60% in two of his four games. That's not great. Freiermuth has a 12.3% target share with 1.16 YPRR, three red zone targets, two deep targets, and a 12.2% first-read share. Freiermuth is only a low-end streaming option this week. Indy is 18th in fantasy points per opportunity allowed to tight ends. He's a touchdown-or-bust option.

Last week, in Jalon Daniels first start, Cade Otton led the team with a 28.6% first-read share while also logging a 22.2% target share (second on the team). Otton was only the TE24 for the week despite the strong usage. He finished with 37 receiving yards, 1.42 YPRR, and zero red zone and deep targets. If Otton sees this type of market share in Week 5, he'll be a strong streaming option. Dallas has allowed the eighth-most yards per target and the third-most fantasy points per opportunity to tight ends. We have seen random big games from Otton in the past, and that could happen again this week.
